reviews.review: The most mind bending, soul crushing, horrifically and psychologically scarring game I have ever played. Never have your choices mattered more than in this game. Just clicking one minor button can change the entire story without realising it. I would 100000000% recommend this game for anyone who wants their mind to be melted

If you ever searched for game where you can be a detective who's choices can prevent the tragedies or cause them then I have a good news for you. That's the game specially for you. Be a part of organisation which spies on people and uses things that it discovered for keeping the peace (in theory). There were moments where I felt bad due to my choices and missing few details. Still, I reccommend playing it to see if you can figure everything without making mistakes.
this game makes me feel like the cia tracking down bin laden in 2007
It's pretty good

This game dives into the moral and ethical boundaries of modern and post modern surveillance. You get to be an investigator that tracks down possible targets, but how far is too far?
The graphics are simple as is audio. But where the game excels is the story. The audio and video are not there to wow or sell the game. I was sucked in when i immediately saw similarities of modern law enforcement techniques taken to a privacy shattering level. 
Within five in-game days, you could be responsible for multiple deaths, government cover ups, and even civil rebellion. The fate of a nation falls into your hands. Choose wisely.

A surprisingly engrossing story that makes you question yourself along the way. At some point, I suspected everyone, and cared about everyone. I made some poor calls and some good calls. It's all a grey area.
Very worth at least one play through, the story engaged and immersed me, even though I was only pointing and clicking. I'm tempted to give it a second play through, but much like learning how a magic trick works, I don't know if the magic will hold up - maybe just to see how the characters interact given different choices.

Great concept, definitely worth picking up and exploring. I think it's as much about the story as the mechanics - which do age faster than you might hope. I feel there could have been 'investigating' than just lifting text from some websites, but still recommend. A 7/10 for me.
Literally 1984, This game gives feeling like a spy and the game is awesome for those who like detective games so play this game if you want a feeling like a spy.

This game's features and methods of story telling dragged me into the world of Orwell almost instantly. The story is very well written and keeps you on your toes up until the very end. The best part is, your actions truly do matter, so make sure to pay attention to what's going on at all times!

Play as yourself using a government surveillance system, Orwell. Investigate the public and private lives of suspect individuals and citizens to find the one responsible for a series of terror attacks and prevent more from ever happening. Moral dilemma nothing, create profiles and collect data to submit to your superiors to bring individuals in for questioning, arrest, or deliver your own type of justice. No one is completely innocent. 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a text based 7+ hour game with 5 chapters and 3 endings. Typically, reading the description of the game it would be natural to suspect Orwell is about learning the evils of government surveillance systems and their terrible effects, but both sides of the issue are shown and the game is very morally ambiguous. There are no right or wrong answers to your choices and honestly, it made the game more interesting. I took my time and ended up playing 9 hours straight instead of the 2-3 I planned. Orwell is remarkably immersive for a game and I definitely recommend you play it if you’re even slightly interested in the story.
10/10 Would invade privacy again
Great investigative game which greatly depicts the dangers and flaws of digital surveillance.

This game is genuinely amazing. I just want to say that I wish that there was 1. a workshop to make your own scenarios (like in 911 operator) and 2. some datachunks that are totally useless, like if when trying to find Goldfel's first name you could say that "A' was his first name - maybe with enough of these there could be an achievement for being completely useless

A really interesting interactive story, pretty captivating and easy to lose yourself in. Does a great job of making things feel looming and ominous. 

My only complaint so far is that sometimes, when you hover over a piece of info to input into a file, it doesn't tell you what it's for or why, which is kind of important to some choices you might make.

fun little dalliance into a style of game that I don't normally play. it's a short game, but thoughtful and decently laid out. if point and click adventures are your thing, you should consider trying Orwell out
Can't wait to try other two endings. Made me scared of national security system again successfully.
Really good game, everyone should play it.

Short game with an interesting concept; that, in my opinion, failed to deliver. For the most part, the game does a good job keeping you guessing if you are making the right choices; but overall, I found the game boring and kept playing only to finish the story, just to be disappointed.

The entire gameplay loop consists of reading and dragging sentences from the right side of the screen to the left. Depending on your choices, the story can move in slightly different directions.

The story was interesting enough to keep me playing. You are an investigator working for a government surveillance system trying to unravel a terrorist group. The game wants you to deal with all the moral struggle that comes with invading people's privacy, but I think the premise falls flat. There were many times throughout the game where I felt it was finally about to get good, but it never materialized. Then the last chapter throws everything overboard: [spoiler] the criminal out themselves undermining all the mystery; the game tries to guilt you into feeling bad for people who had done terrible things; and, for some reason, you are supposed to side with them in the end. [/spoiler]

Too many conflicted opinions to recommend this one. I believe there is a Demo; try it first.

An amazing concept, but the result is disappointing.
1) You do not investigate. You search documents for highlighted clues that you may upload into an investigation database. And you cannot delete them when they turn out to be misleading. Naturally i was careful not to upload dubious claims. Wrong. That gets you stuck. Orwel thrives on rumours, you have to upload these to get new related documents.

2) The writing is boring. The rudimentary gameplay wouldn't matter if the writing was fresh, but the documents you have to go through are as boring as real corporate websites and random people's blogs. Add an annoying coworker and you start regretting you have got that job.

3) The game only pretends to tackle complex issues of privacy and security. The Government is a classical dystopian government that can and will prosecute on "suggestive evidence" which can easily be an off-hand remark of a third party taken out-of-context. If you do not like that, you can side with bomb-throwing anarchists. No third option though, so either way there will be bad outcomes. And that is why surveillance is bad, or so the logic goes.
Philippines under the new presidency simulator.

I clocked in 6 hours total to complete the game. Alright not a lot of game play, but honestly, I’m okay with this because Orwell is a really high-quality game. The music wasn’t grating as some games tend to be, and the UI was very simple, polished, and intuitive. The filters used on the photos of people to give us our character avatars were a bit odd I will admit. (The fishing picture, bruh Josef, wtf are those teeth man?) It made me chuckle a few times, but it really didn’t take away from the quality of the game. As far as game play goes, think of this similar to Papers Please with the addition of choices and story impact. You play as an investigator of the surveillance program called Orwell. You listen to phone calls, read chats, and search the internet for relevant information. This information is then forwarded to your adviser who analyzes your data and acts accordingly. This is where the fun comes in. You can pick and choose what you send to be considered relevant, leaving out certain parts of information, or choosing to mislead the investigation with out of context statements etc. It’s interesting that your choice in data basically drives the story. There’s 5 chapters, so it’s not a lengthy game if you’re not reading through all of the material. The game is very throughout with providing all sorts of tidbits and lore to make it seem like a real program. This isn’t a high-impact gaming experience, more-so an enjoyable romp through the hypotheticals of excessive surveillance and its possible consequences.  This was an interesting as well as thought provoking game, and I appreciate all the thought and effort that was clearly put into it. I would surely recommend this to casual gamers. If you’re into shooting zombies on repeat and yelling jokes about sleeping with mothers, this probably isn’t for you. 8/10

It's an interesting concept, but after the first one or two hours the game fails to deliver more than that. It soon just carries out into dragging data chunks around, without introducing more twists to the gameplay to keep the game enjoyable. The story is alright, but isn't backed up by good gameplay enough to shine at all.

This is a short but sweet point-and-click story game that does a great job of illustrating the horrific consequences of building a justice system based upon highly intrusive mass surveillance.   

Probably the best thing about this game is how good it is at playing against your own personal biases.  You may think that you have all the answers and that you're making a just decision but then the plot twists and you find yourself opening a whole realm of possibilities.  

A further addition to this confusion is the supervisor who monitors you and compels you to do a good job, but eventually you start experiencing serious consequences that make you question the ethics of the entire operation. 

While this game doesn't take long to finish, there are multiple endings that make replaying it enjoyable since you will know most if not all of the truth depending on how observant you were.  

One more thing to add:  don't be afraid of making a "wrong" decision because part of the fun is seeing what happens as a result. 

I highly recommend this game.

For such a simple UI it's incredibly buggy. Half the time popups that you need to make smart decisions don't appear. I managed to softlock the game during Episode 4 out of 5, and there's no way to restart a specific chapter without beating the entire game first, so to get past it I'd have to replay the entire game and hopefully not hit that bug again. Without the rampant technical issues it'd be a cool game but as is it's just a disappointing waste of cash. If you're looking for a good game in this genre have a look at Greyhat instead.

This is a narrative game in which the story develops through websites, private text and phone conversations and files in computers. You are able to access all of this as an employee of a state surveilance apparatus, and while the story is mostly linear you do get the chance to affect its development by choosing which information you pass on to the system and which you don't.

It's quite an interesting game, with a good, twisty story and pleasant music and aesthetics. It is a bit slow at times, but all in all I enjoyed the experience.

9/10

Pretty unique take on point and click mechanics in a visual novel style game. Choices are hard to make, whether that be due to the actual choice or how you go about making it. A lot of reading but it is very engaging and thought-provoking.

I don't have the best eye sight, and even with my glasses on and my laptop only 2 feet from my face, I found myself squinting to see the text the majority of the time. It was low contrast and there was no way to make the text bigger.

That being said, the game itself I did enjoy. It's an interesting exercise in the dangers of excessive governmental surveillance a la Orwell's book 1984. You play as an investigator looking to incriminate various persons of interest in a terrorist attack, and quickly discover that there is no way to be free of bias and it's very easy to make human errors, possibly leading to the arrest of the wrong person. The answer is not always simple.

It's interesting to see what aspects cause you to have certain biases.

The game was short; I finished it in about 4 hours. But I want to replay it eventually to pick different options to see where they lead me. It certainly has replay value in addition to its message, and the story is quite interesting. It's nice to sit down and finish a game in one evening. I recommend checking it out unless you have vision issues like me.

The soundtrack is very solid, and the controls are very easy to follow.

It's a brilliant game. You're in charge of analysing data on people, and giving chunks of that data to authorities, to try and find out who is bombing public areas. The data you choose to give or not give to the authorities will have an impact on some of the peoples lives, and also the ending of the game. It's very unique and I highly recommend it. It definitely has replayability. I have played through it twice, a couple of years apart, and the second time I had completely forgotten the plot, which was nice.

Very inaccessible for those with visual disabilities, there are literally no accessibility settings to change font size, ui scale, background colours, etc.
 The white background prevalent makes it extremely hard for those who suffer from photo-sensitivity. This can slightly be resolved through accessibility features native to Windows such as high contrast colours and magnifiers, however this does not lead to the same gameplay experience as those who are not affected by these and is extremely inconvenient.

It seems to be a simple fix to allow at least UI scale and option for a dark mode, which would also benefit players who are playing late at night, for example. It's a simple fix but this game is extremely hard for me to play due to lack of basic accessibility features, which is a shame because I was actually looking forward to playing this.

Splendid and thought-provoking game in this digital era. Electronic surveillance may be justified on the grounds of crime prevention and anti-terrorism, but it comes at a heavy price. I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?
